newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia sees Natuna gas output in 2003.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia sees Natuna gas output in 2003.

text.p: Indonesia's state-owned Pertamina is optimistic its huge Natuna gas project will hit first production in 2003, but analysts said the company must move fast to reach that target.
They said Pertamina needs to secure gas sales quickly to get what is logistically a difficult project moving forward.

But G.A.S. Nayoan, senior executive vice president at Pertamina for gas field development, said in an interview with Reuters: "We have always been optimistic since we started the project...there is demand but it depends on willing sellers' and willing buyers' attitude."

Natuna is one of the world's biggest gas fields with reserves of 222 trillion cubic feet. But a high carbon dioxide (Co2) level of 71.8 percent means that actual recoverable reserves are estimated at 46 trillion cubic feet.
Nayoan said the estimate of reserves was likely to rise once a planned two-year seismic test was completed.

He said competition for gas that would be available in the first decade of the next century was increasing but Pertamina had driven Natuna's costs down to below $4 per British Thermal Unit (BTU) in the past three years.
Analysts said this pricing would make Natuna competitive with other projects due onstream at the same time.
Nayoan forecast first production in 2003 at 480 million cubic feet per day (mcfd), doubling the following year.
Maximum production would be hit in 2007 at 2.4 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd).
But analysts said that timetable was optimistic, adding that Natuna faced a number of uncertainties.
The project was large to start with and would require huge financing of up to $40 billion. The high level of redundant Co2 had to be moved.
In addition, Australia, Qatar, Oman and possibly Yemen would be looking to market LNG at the same time, which was likely to add to cost pressures, analysts said.
"2003 sounds extremely optimistic," said one analyst, who requested anonymity. "There are such huge problems in dealing with a project of this size...it's going to be tricky."

"There is a lot of LNG coming to the market at the same time," he said. "Potentially, there could be an oversupply. If you have a project like Natuna, where you are throwing away 70 percent of what you produce, you have to question how you would compete."

So far, Natuna shareholders Pertamina (24 percent), Mobil Corp (26 percent) and Exxon Corp (50 percent) have secured a memorandum of understanding to sell Thailand 500 mcfd of piped gas from the field in 2005 and 2006. Thailand also wants to acquire an 11-15 percent stake in the field.
Analysts said the project critically needs a sales agreement with big LNG buyers like Japan or South Korea to help raise confidence in the project and secure financing.

However, Indonesia's Pertamina is a world leader in LNG and Mobil and Exxon are two of the most experienced companies in the upstream gas sector, which will help drive the project forward, the analysts said.
"Pertamina has to be forward. It has to be seen driving the project forward," one analyst said.
